    Overview

         Recently, the RBI released the June 2026 edition of the Financial Stability Report (FSR).
       The FSR report reflects the collective assessment of the Sub-Committee of the
         Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC) on risks to financial stability and
        the resilience of the Indian financial system.

     About the FSR Report

           Released by: RBI

          FSR is a bi-annual publication

           Prepared after taking into account the contributions from all the financial sector
             regulators

            Reflects the collective assessment of the Sub-Committee of the Financial Stability
          and Development Council (FSDC) on risks to financial stability and the resilience of
           the financial system.

          As a part of FSR, RBI also conducts Systemic Risk Survey (SRS), which assesses the
              financial system on 5 different types of risks — Global, Financial, Macroeconomic,
             Institutional and General.

      Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC)

       The FSDC is a high-level body set up by the Government of India in 2010 (not a
         statutory body) to:

            Maintain financial stability in India,

           Promote financial sector development,

           Coordinate between different financial regulators.

           Ensures coordination among regulators and looks at macro-financial risks (like
               inflation, currency crisis, banking stress).

           Discusses policy issues affecting financial stability, inclusion, and literacy.

           Supports development of the financial sector, especially during crisis periods.

              It was set up on the recommendation of the Raghuram Rajan Committee (2008) on
         financial sector reforms.

          The Union Finance Minister is the Chairperson of FSDC.





Financial Stability Report (June 2026)                                                                                                   2

It includes heads of all major financial sector regulators:

           RBI Governor

           SEBI Chairperson

           IRDAI Chairperson

         PFRDA Chairperson

           Finance Secretary

           Chief Economic Adviser (CEA)

           Secretary of the DEA and MoF

    FSDC Sub-Committee

          The Sub-Committee of FSDC is the operational arm of FSDC.

                    It handles the technical and implementation work of FSDC decisions.

          The RBI Governor is the Chairperson of the FSDC Sub-Committee.

     Focus Areas of Sub-Committee

            Risk management in banks and financial institutions,

            Cybersecurity in financial systems,

             Crisis preparedness and coordination during financial shocks,

            Supervision of financial conglomerates,

             Financial fraud detection and mitigation

     Highlights of the Report

        (A) Global financial system: Despite recent global shocks, including the West Asia
         conflict, the global financial system has remained largely stable after an initial period
         of market volatility.

           However, global financial stability risks remain elevated due to:

              Supply chain disruptions could increase inflation and tighten financial conditions.

              High public debt across countries.

                 Fragile bond markets.

               Elevated asset valuations.

              High leverage among Non-Bank Financial Intermediaries (NBFIs).

         (B) Indian financial system:





Financial Stability Report (June 2026)                                                                                                   3

India remains better placed than many other economies because of its strong
          macroeconomic fundamentals, making it more resilient to external shocks.

          The balance of risks has improved, supported by:

                the interim peace agreement in West Asia, and

              Recent measures taken by the Government of India and the RBI have been to
                  attract capital inflows.

          The Indian financial system remains resilient due to the strong financial position of
           both banks and non-bank financial institutions.

          Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs) continue to remain financially sound because
              of:

               Strong capital and liquidity buffers,

               Improving asset quality (lower NPAs), and

                Stable profitability.

            RBI's macro stress tests indicate that even under severe adverse scenarios, banks
            are expected to maintain capital levels well above the minimum regulatory
           requirement.

          Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) also remain healthy, supported by:

               Strong capital position, Good profitability, and improving asset quality.

          The insurance sector continues to remain stable, with the solvency ratio of life
            insurers staying above the prescribed regulatory minimum.

    Chapter I: Macrofinancial Risks

     Global outlook

      OECD Countries' Refinancing Needs (2025):

           Refinancing means repaying old debt by borrowing new debt.

              In 2025, OECD countries need to refinance US$13.5 trillion of debt—a record high.

            This amount is about 80% of all the money they plan to borrow in 2025.

      Why is this a concern?

      Many governments are issuing short-term bonds instead of long-term bonds.

        This means they have to repay debt more frequently and borrow again at whatever
         interest rate exists at that time. If interest rates rise or investors lose confidence,
       governments may face:

           Higher borrowing costs.





Financial Stability Report (June 2026)                                                                                                   4

Difficulty refinancing their debt.

            Greater financial risk.

        How the West Asia conflict affected India specifically:

          The West Asia conflict hit India through the financial channel in 3 ways:

              1. Exchange rate (INR) → came under depreciation pressure.

Microfinance Sector

       The Microfinance Sector provides small loans and basic financial services to low-
       income individuals and households who usually do not have access to traditional bank
        loans. In India, microfinance is provided by:

              Microfinance Institutions (MFIs)

              Small Finance Banks (SFBs)

             Commercial Banks

            NBFC-MFIs (Non-Banking Financial Company–Microfinance Institutions)

               Self-Help Groups (SHGs) linked with banks

        Outlook:

            Credit growth has turned positive, marking the first expansion after a prolonged
           slowdown.

           Asset quality is improving, as fewer loans are overdue.

           Over-leveraging has reduced, with fewer borrowers taking loans from multiple
             lenders.

           However, the borrower base continues to shrink, indicating that fewer households

    NBFC Sector

          1. Strong Financial Position: The NBFC sector remains resilient, supported by strong
             capitalisation, healthy Net Interest Margins (NIMs), sustained profitability, and
           improving asset quality due to declining NPAs.

          2. Credit Growth: Overall credit growth has moderated, indicating a slowdown in total
            lending compared to previous years.

          3. Retail Lending: Despite slower overall credit growth, retail lending remains robust
          and has become the primary driver of NBFC credit expansion.

          4. Gold Loans: The sharp increase in gold loans has fueled retail lending, with gold
            loans now accounting for 17.4% of the NBFCs' retail loan portfolio.

          5. Credit Costs: Credit costs have continued to decline, meaning NBFCs are making
            lower provisions for bad loans due to improving repayment performance.





Financial Stability Report (June 2026)                                                                                                  11

Analysis of the chart

          1. GNPA (Asset Quality): GNPA has steadily improved from ~5.6% (Mar-22) to 2.4%
            (Mar-26), showing strong and sustained improvement in asset quality.

          2. NIM (Margins): Net Interest Margin has strengthened from ~4.3% to 5.1%,
            remaining near multi-year highs, indicating stable and strong profitability from
             lending.

          3. ROA (Profitability): ROA rose sharply to a peak of ~2.9%, but has slightly eased to
          2.3%, still indicating healthy profitability despite minor moderation.

          4. CRAR (Capital): CRAR has declined from a peak of ~27.5% (2023) to 24.6%
            (2026), but remains well above regulatory norms, though the downward trend needs
            monitoring.

      NBFCs are relying more on banks, less on foreign currency

          1. More bank loans: NBFCs are now borrowing more from Indian banks instead of
            other sources.

          2. Safer funding: Bank loans are more stable and reliable, so NBFCs’ funding position
           has improved.





Financial Stability Report (June 2026)                                                                                                  12

3. Lower cost: Borrowing from banks is also cheaper, so NBFCs save money on
              interest costs.

          4. Why less foreign borrowing:

                        If the rupee falls, foreign loans become expensive to repay.

             Hedging (insurance against currency risk) is also costly.

               So when NBFCs borrow in foreign currency, they worry that if the rupee
               weakens (falls), they will need more rupees to repay the same foreign loan.

       Asset Quality in NBFCs: Two-Speed Improvement (ML vs UL)

          1. NBFC-ML (Middle Layer): Asset quality is improving clearly, with slippage ratios
              falling from earlier peaks, showing better loan repayment behaviour.

                a. Slippage ratio = Fresh bad loans created during a period.

          2. NBFC-UL (Upper Layer): Asset quality is still under pressure, as slippages remain
             relatively high, although there are early signs of stabilisation.

          3. Overall Sector Position: The Net NPA ratio has declined to 0.8%, indicating that
             overall bad loans in the NBFC sector are at a low level.

Financial Stability Report (June 2026)                                                                                                  14

1. Earnings slowdown: Bank profits are slowing. NII growth has fallen sharply to 4%
        (from double digits earlier), and PAT growth has slowed to 7.2% (from 16.8%). This is
        mainly because interest margins are getting squeezed as interest rates fall.

         2. Higher concentration risk: Banks are lending more to a smaller set of borrowers,
       which increases risk, meaning credit is becoming less diversified.

         3. Interest rate risk (especially Foreign Banks): Foreign banks are highly sensitive to
         rate changes. A 250 bps rate shock would reduce their capital sharply (CRAR down by
       588 bps), much worse than PSBs and private banks. Two foreign banks could fall below
        the safe capital limit.

         4. Trading losses: All bank groups faced losses in securities trading, with foreign
       banks losing for four straight quarters, showing pressure from market volatility.

         5. Stress test risks: Even though the banking system is strong overall, stress tests show
         that a small number of banks (especially foreign banks) could become weak under
        extreme financial shocks, both in capital and liquidity. A stress test checks what will
       happen to banks if the economy faces a very bad situation (like a big rise in bad loans or
         financial shock). Under a severe stress scenario:

         4 banks may fall below the minimum capital requirement (CRAR)

         2 foreign banks may fail the liquidity requirement (LCR)

     Cooperative Banks (UCBs)

          1. Overall improvement: UCB sector is improving overall, but mid-sized cooperative
          banks (Tier 2 and Tier 3) are still weak and may fail under severe financial stress,
            especially due to interest rate shocks.

          2. Hidden weakness:

         When a severe interest rate shock in trading books is assumed:

              10 Tier 2 UCBs may fall below the minimum capital (CRAR)

                  11 Tier 3 UCBs may fall below the minimum capital (CRAR)

          3. Tier-wise difference:

                Tier 1 and Tier 4 UCBs: Strong and stable → no major impact in stress scenarios

                Tier 2 and Tier 3 UCBs: Weak point → show real vulnerability

Insurance Sector

           1. Life Insurance: More policyholders are surrendering or withdrawing their policies
         early. Surrenders now account for 38.3% of total payouts, almost equal to maturity
         benefits (36.9%). This makes it difficult for insurers to manage their long-term funds
         (Asset-Liability Management or ALM).

         2. Higher Costs: Private life insurers are paying higher commissions to agents, which is
        reducing their profit margins.

         3. General Insurance Losses: General insurers continue to make losses from their core
        insurance business (underwriting). Public sector insurers recorded an underwriting
         loss of ₹31,000 crore in 2025–26.





Financial Stability Report (June 2026)                                                                                                  17

4. Dependence on Investments: Most general insurers are earning profits from
        investment income rather than from selling insurance policies, which is not a
         sustainable source of profitability.

         5. Weak Solvency: Three general insurers have remained below the minimum
        solvency requirement (150%) for five consecutive quarters, indicating persistent
         financial weakness.

         6. Rising Customer Complaints: Policyholder grievances have increased sharply from
        0.65 lakh to 1.78 lakh over the last five years, highlighting concerns about service
          quality.

           7. Stress Test Results: Under severe financial stress, only 4 of the top 10 life insurers
       and 3–4 of the top 10 general insurers would continue to meet the required solvency
        norms. This shows that some insurers have limited capital to absorb major shocks.

     Systemic Interconnectedness

          1. Stronger Linkages: Financial institutions are becoming more connected, with total
          exposures between 280 institutions increasing by 20.1% over the previous year.

          2. Major Borrowers: NBFCs, private banks, and housing finance companies (HFCs)
            are the largest borrowers of funds in the financial system.

          3. Major Lenders: Mutual funds (AMC-MFs), insurance companies, and public sector
          banks (PSBs) are the largest providers of funds.

          4. Contagion Risk: Because institutions are closely connected, financial problems in
          one institution can spread to others. However, the current level of contagion risk
           remains low and manageable.

          5. Stress Test Results: RBI's stress tests show that even if one bank fails, the overall
           impact on the banking system would be limited, with only a small reduction in capital
          and only one additional bank likely to be affected under combined stress.

    Chapter III: Regulatory Initiatives in the
     Financial Sector

     Global Regulatory Developments

          1. Global Background: Global uncertainties such as trade disruptions, geopolitical
             tensions, volatile energy prices, and changing capital flows have increased risks to
            the financial system. Therefore, regulators across the world have introduced new
          measures since December 2025 to strengthen financial stability, improve risk
          management, and simplify regulatory frameworks.





Financial Stability Report (June 2026)                                                                                                  18

2. Basel III Monitoring Report (BCBS): The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision
          (BCBS) reported that globally, banks continue to maintain stable capital and leverage
              ratios, while their liquidity position has improved slightly.

          3. Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR): The report noted that the average Liquidity
          Coverage Ratio (LCR) of large international banks increased slightly, indicating that
          banks are better prepared to meet short-term financial stress.

          4. Basel III Output Floor: Countries are gradually implementing the Basel III Output
             Floor, which prevents banks from reducing capital requirements excessively by
            using their own internal risk models. The minimum capital requirement under this
           framework will reach 72.5% by January 2028.

          5. Operational Risk Framework: The BCBS issued a technical amendment to the
           Standardised Approach for Operational Risk, clarifying how business indicators
           should be used to calculate operational risk capital. Member countries are expected
             to implement these changes within three years.

          6. Synthetic Risk Transfers (SRT): The BCBS reviewed the increasing use of Synthetic
            Risk Transfers (SRTs), such as Credit Default Swaps (CDS) and Credit-Linked
          Notes (CLNs), which allow banks to transfer credit risk without selling the underlying
             loans.

          7. Need for Stronger Supervision: The BCBS emphasised that regulators should
             closely supervise SRT transactions because they increase the interconnectedness
          between banks and non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs), which may create
              financial stability risks.

          8. FSB Resolution Report: The Financial Stability Board (FSB) reviewed global
           progress in improving resolution frameworks for banks, insurance companies, and
              financial market infrastructures. The report highlighted improvements in crisis
          management planning and the ability of institutions to be resolved without disrupting
            the financial system.

          9. Recovery and Resolution Planning for Insurers: The FSB issued final guidance
            containing six criteria to help regulators identify which insurance companies should
           prepare recovery and resolution plans, ensuring that failures can be managed
           smoothly without affecting policyholders or the financial system.

        10. FSB Annual Report: The FSB stated that it will review why the implementation of
         G20 financial reforms has slowed in recent years and will focus on improving the
              effective implementation of global regulatory reforms to maintain financial stability.

       Decentralised Finance (DeFi) and Digital Assets

          1. Growing Importance of Stablecoins: Stablecoins are receiving increased attention
           from global regulators because they are becoming more closely connected with
              traditional financial markets, payment systems, and government securities.





Financial Stability Report (June 2026)                                                                                                  19

2. Stablecoin Issuers Holding Reserve Assets: Stablecoin issuers are increasingly
             investing in traditional reserve assets such as government securities, making them
          an important part of the financial system and requiring closer regulatory monitoring.

          3. MF Findings on Stablecoins: According to the IMF's Global Financial Stability
           Report (2026), cross-border stablecoin transactions have grown rapidly, especially
              in emerging market economies.

          4. Use of Stablecoins: Stablecoin transactions are closely linked with:

              Crypto asset market activity.

                 International remittances.

               Cross-border trade.

          5. Why Stablecoins Are Popular: Demand for stablecoins is generally higher in
            countries with:

            Weak institutions.

                   Political instability.

                Limited access to short-term US dollar assets.

          6. Benefits and Risks of Stablecoins: Stablecoins can make cross-border payments
             faster and provide access to US dollar-denominated assets. However, they also
            create concerns about currency substitution, monetary sovereignty, and financial
               stability.

          7. Global Regulatory Developments: Several jurisdictions have introduced dedicated
            regulatory frameworks for stablecoins, including:

               United States – GENIUS Act

             European Union – MiCA Framework

               United Kingdom – Proposed Stablecoin Regulatory Regime

          These initiatives aim to provide greater regulatory clarity and consumer protection.

          8. International Organisation of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) 2026 Work
         Programme plans to:

              Develop a common methodology for assessing crypto assets.

              Conduct regular thematic reviews across countries.

               Monitor developments in tokenisation and other financial technologies.

                Issue supervisory guidance on Artificial Intelligence (AI) governance and
                  financial disclosures.

          9. Basel Committee and FSB Initiatives: The Basel Committee on Banking
           Supervision (BCBS) and the Financial Stability Board (FSB) have identified digital





Financial Stability Report (June 2026)                                                                                                  20

finance as a key priority. Their focus includes:

               Monitoring crypto asset markets.

               Implementing prudential standards for crypto assets.

              Addressing cross-border risks associated with digital assets.

        10. Objective: These global initiatives seek to promote innovation while ensuring that
                digital assets and stablecoins do not threaten financial stability, consumer
              protection, or the effectiveness of financial regulation.

      Climate Finance

          1. IMF Technical Note on Climate Risk: The International Monetary Fund (IMF)
            published a technical note explaining how climate-related risks should be
            incorporated into financial regulation and banking supervision.

          2. Global Standard-Setting Bodies: The IMF reviewed the work of major international
             organisations, including:

           BCBS (Basel Committee on Banking Supervision)

           NGFS (Network for Greening the Financial System)

              ISSB (International Sustainability Standards Board)

            FSB (Financial Stability Board)

        During the review period, Indian financial regulators introduced several measures to

          1. Directions on Lending to Related Parties:

          The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) observed that lending to related parties may create
             conflicts of interest and lead to unfair lending decisions.

              In January 2026, the RBI issued principle-based Directions on Related Party
           Lending to ensure that lending decisions remain independent, and in the interest of
            the bank and its stakeholders.

2. Risk-Based Premium Framework for Deposit Insurance:

          The Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC), with RBI
            approval, introduced a Risk-Based Premium (RBP) Framework under the DICGC
            Act, 1961.

                           i. Two-Tier Risk Assessment: The framework classifies banks into:

                    Tier 1: Scheduled Commercial Banks (excluding Regional Rural Banks).

                    Tier 2: Regional Rural Banks, Rural Cooperative Banks, and Urban
                  Cooperative Banks.

                          ii. Premium Linked to Risk: Instead of charging every bank the same premium, the
            new framework links the deposit insurance premium to the bank's risk profile.

                         iii. Vintage Discount: Banks that have contributed to the Deposit Insurance Fund
                 (DIF) for many years without any insurance claim payout receive a vintage
               discount, allowing them to pay a lower premium.

          3. Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI) in Debt Securities:

          From 1 April 2026, investments made by FPIs under the Voluntary Retention Route
           (VRR) are counted under the respective investment limits of the General Route.

            FPIs investing under VRR can now partially or fully liquidate their investments after
           completing the minimum retention period, even if they originally committed to a
            longer investment period.
